name: Noche de Dados: Jeffrey como Director

sentences.base_language: It's Saturday night and Jeffrey's brothers arrive at his house with snacks and dice.
sentences.target_language: Es sábado por la noche y los hermanos de Jeffrey llegan a su casa con bocadillos y dados.
sentences.grammarNote:
**Es sábado** — **ser** is always used for days of the week and times: **Es lunes**, **Son las ocho**.
**bocadillos** = snacks (literally 'little bites' in Latin American Spanish — from **bocado**, a bite). In Spain, **bocadillo** specifically means a baguette sandwich.

sentences.base_language: Jeffrey is the dungeon master tonight.
sentences.target_language: Esta noche, Jeffrey es el director del juego.
sentences.grammarNote:
**es el director del juego** — **ser** for roles and identities: being the dungeon master is Jeffrey's role/function for this session.
**del juego** = of the game — **del** = mandatory contraction of **de + el**.

sentences.base_language: He has been preparing the campaign for three weeks.
sentences.target_language: Lleva tres semanas preparando la campaña.
sentences.grammarNote:
**Lleva + time + gerund** = has been [doing something] for [time] — a very common Spanish construction for ongoing actions: **Llevo dos horas estudiando** (I've been studying for two hours).
**preparando** = preparing — gerund of **preparar** (-ar verb, remove -ar add -ando).

sentences.base_language: His notes, maps, and monster cards cover the entire table.
sentences.target_language: Sus notas, mapas y tarjetas de monstruos cubren toda la mesa.
sentences.grammarNote:
**cubren** = cover (third-person plural of **cubrir**, regular -ir). Past participle: **cubierto** (irregular).
**toda la mesa** = the entire table — **todo/toda + definite article + noun** = all/the entire: **todo el día** (all day), **toda la semana** (all week).

sentences.base_language: 'Okay, everyone. Read your character sheets. We begin in five minutes.'
sentences.target_language: —Bien, todos. Lean sus fichas de personaje. Empezamos en cinco minutos.
sentences.grammarNote:
**Lean** = Read (ustedes affirmative imperative of **leer**): the imperative of **leer** in ustedes is **lean** — irregular because of the vowel shift in the stem.
**fichas de personaje** = character sheets — **ficha** (card/form) is a common term; some groups say **hojas de personaje** (character sheets/leaves).

sentences.base_language: One brother plays a warrior and the other plays a wizard.
sentences.target_language: Un hermano juega de guerrero y el otro juega de mago.
sentences.grammarNote:
**jugar de** = to play as [a character class] — **jugar** (o→ue stem-changing: juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, jugáis, juegan). Preterite yo: **jugué** (g→gu before e).
**el otro** = the other — **otro** does not use an indefinite article in Spanish: **un otro** is incorrect; say **otro** or **el otro**.

sentences.base_language: Jeffrey describes the scene in a dramatic voice: 'You find yourselves in a dark tavern...'
sentences.target_language: Jeffrey describe la escena en voz dramática: —Se encuentran en una taberna oscura…
sentences.grammarNote:
**describe** = describes (él/ella present of **describir**, regular -ir).
**Se encuentran** = You find yourselves — reflexive **encontrarse** (to find oneself/be located). The ustedes form sets the immersive DM narration tone; **se encuentran en** is the standard phrase for placing characters in a scene.

sentences.base_language: 'Wait — can my warrior carry a magic bow? I think the rules allow it.'
sentences.target_language: —Espera, ¿puede mi guerrero llevar un arco mágico? Creo que las reglas lo permiten.
sentences.grammarNote:
**puede** = can (él/ella present of **poder**, o→ue): puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden.
**Creo que** = I think/believe that — **creer** (to believe) is a regular -er verb; **creo** is the yo form. **Creo que + indicative** (not subjunctive) because it expresses a personal belief, not doubt.

sentences.base_language: 'No, warriors can't use bows in this campaign,' Jeffrey says firmly.
sentences.target_language: —No, los guerreros no pueden usar arcos en esta campaña —dice Jeffrey con firmeza.
sentences.grammarNote:
**no pueden usar** = can't use — **poder + infinitive** for ability; negated with **no** before **pueden**.
**con firmeza** = firmly — noun **firmeza** (firmness) preceded by **con** (with) to form an adverbial phrase; a natural Spanish alternative to adverbs in -mente.

sentences.base_language: His brother rolls his eyes but accepts the ruling.
sentences.target_language: Su hermano pone los ojos en blanco pero acepta la decisión.
sentences.grammarNote:
**poner los ojos en blanco** = to roll one's eyes — a fixed expression (literally 'to put the eyes in white/blank').
**la decisión** = the ruling/decision — **decisión** is feminine: **la decisión**, plural **las decisiones** (accent drops in plural).

sentences.base_language: The session goes on for four hours.
sentences.grammarNote:
**dura** = lasts (él/ella present of **durar**, regular -ar).
**cuatro horas** = four hours — no preposition needed in Spanish when stating a duration with a verb like **durar**: **La película dura dos horas** (The film lasts two hours).

sentences.base_language: Jeffrey rolls dice behind his screen, building the suspense.
sentences.target_language: Jeffrey tira los dados detrás de su pantalla, creando suspenso.
sentences.grammarNote:
**tira** = rolls (él/ella present of **tirar**, regular -ar) — common verb for rolling dice, literally 'to throw'.
**creando suspenso** = building suspense — gerund of **crear** used to describe a simultaneous action. **Suspenso** (suspense) is also the word for 'failing grade' in Spain — context makes the meaning clear.

sentences.base_language: 'I need you to roll a perception check,' Jeffrey says to his brother.
sentences.target_language: —Necesito que hagas una tirada de percepción —le dice Jeffrey a su hermano.
sentences.grammarNote:
**necesito que hagas** — **necesitar que + subjunctive**: **hagas** is the tú present subjunctive of **hacer** (to do/make), used because Jeffrey is expressing a need for his brother to do something.
**tirada** = roll/throw (feminine noun from **tirar**): **una tirada de dado** = a dice roll.

sentences.base_language: His brother rolls a three. 'You notice nothing unusual.'
sentences.target_language: Su hermano saca un tres. —No notas nada inusual.
sentences.grammarNote:
**saca un tres** = rolls a three — **sacar** used colloquially for getting a score on a die (see main vocabulary cards).
**No notas nada inusual** — double negative is required in Spanish: **nada** (nothing) with a negated verb **no notas** = you notice nothing. In Spanish, multiple negatives reinforce rather than cancel each other.

sentences.base_language: Everyone laughs. Bean, Jeffrey's Pomeranian, runs across the map.
sentences.target_language: Todos se ríen. Bean, el Pomerania de Jeffrey, corre por encima del mapa.
sentences.grammarNote:
**se ríen** = they laugh — reflexive verb **reírse** (to laugh), third-person plural. **Reírse** is an e→i stem-changing verb: me río, te ríes, se ríe, nos reímos, os reís, se ríen.
**por encima de** = across/over — literally 'through above of'; a very useful preposition of position/movement.

sentences.base_language: It was the best D&D session they'd had in months.
sentences.target_language: Fue la mejor sesión de D&D que habían tenido en meses.
sentences.grammarNote:
**Fue** = it was — preterite of **ser** (to be): fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron. **Ser** and **ir** share the same preterite forms — context makes them distinct.
**que habían tenido** = that they had had — past perfect (pluperfect): **haber (habían)** + past participle **tenido**, used for an action completed before another past event.
